events.title: recomp/mdamiga: colours grouped by how much of the screen shows them; sprites behind plane B's cells with priority. The fifteen slots of a playfield went to the colours farthest apart, so a rare bright one took a slot and the dark ones a stage is mostly made of shared one (Thunder Force IV's Air-raid: a grey sky with black boxes where it should be black; the panels' black gone brown). Now a colour weighs what the cells drawn with its tiles come to, the slots are picked by distance times weight and moved to the middle of their colours three times, and a slot's colour is the weighted mean. Sprites without priority are cut by the pixels of plane B's cells with priority (the stage select's pictures, which showed whole over the panel). recomp host: RECOMP_POKE=ADDR:VAL,... holds bytes every frame (lives, so a scripted run plays through for the analysis)

events.title: agk port: scratch below the stack pointer goes to the layer's page. Thunder Force IV's DMA routine does movea.l sp,a0 and splits the length into bytes through -(a0) and (a0)+ without moving the stack; on the Amiga the layer's interrupts come at any time and their frame lands there (the length's low byte came back as $6C, the frame's vector offset: a transfer too long by that much ran over the game's empty tile, and cells of rubbish spread over both planes on a slow machine). recomp/mdamiga: the blitter's sprites are on again. What the blitter can copy it copies: a cell is written to chip RAM once by the CPU and handed on to the other bitmaps, all of that and the putting back of sprites done before the CPU writes cells, the sprites in a second go. The VDP's state held across the game's handlers includes what a DMA is set up with and is kept on the stack around each handler (they nest, and this game's first one never returns). Cell rows are gone through from where the last pass stopped and the planes take turns; a colour seen for the first time with no close slot is grouped soon. Debug: -DDBG_WATCH=addr says who writes that VRAM, the F1 dump takes the layer's marks and shadow. Stock A1200: the demo's logic at about 67%

events.title: recomp/mdamiga: the blitter draws the sprites, the bitplanes are fetched 64 bits at a time, planes taller than the bitmaps. The bitmaps' lines hold their four planes one after the other, so one blit cuts a sprite into plane A (its image and mask kept in chip RAM, made once) and one puts back what it covered from a copy of plane A without sprites; a picture's blits are a queue the blitter's interrupt works through and the picture is shown when the last is done, never begun again before the blank that shows it. Sprites behind cells with priority or across a change of line scroll are still drawn by hand. FMODE 3 with the scroll's two extra bits: the bitplanes take 15% of the bus instead of 53%. The window's bitmap is laid out as the playfields' are (no pointer moves on its lines). A plane of 64 or 128 cell rows is seen through the bitmap's 32, each bitmap row holding the plane row in view (Thunder Force IV's stages scroll up and down: rows of the wrong cells before). Colours are grouped again only when the fit got worse than the last grouping left it, each time after twice the wait. The layer's page and its cell move to fast RAM with the code. Stock A1200: the demo's logic at about 60% of full speed

events.title: agk port: a stop says it is asleep. The byte after the layer's cell is set before each stop and cleared when the Amiga's interrupt entry gives the game an interrupt; an interrupt of the Amiga's own puts the game back into the stop only while it is set. The return address alone is the same just after a wake, so a copper interrupt landing between the game's handler and the next instruction sent Thunder Force IV back to sleep for good (frozen on a demo's GAME OVER or the ranking, depending on timing). RECOMP_Z80_SILENT=1: the checking build's Z80 RAM reads 0, as on a port with no sound

events.title: agk port: a second game. Thunder Force IV matches the original on 7997 of 8000 frames on the host and reaches its first stage on the Amiga. What it needed: a stack from address 0 is the top of RAM; stop's interrupt mask is lowered and on the Amiga an interrupt the game didn't get puts it back to sleep; a call with its data after it keeps the old return address; rte is the 68000's (move (sp)+,sr; rts) and the Amiga's interrupt entry builds frames to match; tables of routines behind a base register and routine addresses stored as immediates are followed (14,000 to 42,000 instructions); old bytes that never ran are neither patched nor poisoned; $A10001 answers the region the header asks for. The checking build looks at the chips' events where the original's control flow was (Sonic 2 now matches on all 4000 frames) and has RECOMP_PORT_STOP and RECOMP_DUMP_AT; an unhandled exception on the Amiga is reported on the serial port

agk port: the game runs first and the picture is drawn in its waits. The loops where the game waits for an interrupt are found (a test of RAM and a branch back to it) and listed for the layer; the copper raises an interrupt every sixteen lines and, when it lands in one, the layer draws until the blank is near. The VDP's status reads in-blank while the game's vertical interrupt runs (Sonic 2's handler waited a frame for the flag when the Amiga delivered it late). DMA to video memory compared and copied in longs, scroll geometry only when its inputs change, tiles to planar through a table per palette line, whole sprite cells a tile row at a time. Stock A1200 with fast RAM, sound off: Emerald Hill's logic from about 30% of full speed to 70-90%. README: the Mega Drive port

last_commit.message: NFS_DOS.EXE of EA's 1997 CD accepted too (a player's: "not the version ReNFS knows"). Its build, dated 17 June 1996, the same 1,254,591 bytes, differs from the 19 June one laid out and relocated only in the give-up branch of keys_control_word 0x48bec (the word written 0x000087a0, not 0xffff87a0; the function 4 bytes longer) and one German text at 0xe3814, neither read by the port: exe.c takes either FNV-1a (0x76078ed2, 0x21ef7c33). With every read checked against those bytes, the 1997 CD drew the same pictures in the front end, the four replays (equal at every snapshot) and nine races. Our CD copy has three bits flipped where the 1997 CD's bytes match their neighbours (NOTES §1). The message no longer says 1996.
